meta.title: Turkish A1
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Turkish → English (see the Turkish, recall the meaning) and English → Turkish (see an English meaning, recall the Turkish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for level A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: the Yunus Emre Institute's Turkish Proficiency Exam (TYS) certifies only B2 and C1 and publishes no vocabulary list. The scope of this deck is taken instead from the Turkish as a Foreign Language Teaching Programme (Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı; Türkiye Maarif Foundation, 2nd edition, 2020, approved by Turkey's Ministry of National Education), a CEFR-based syllabus whose A1 tables for secondary school (pp. 243–254) list vocabulary under ten themes: introductions, the classroom, family and home, a daily routine, getting about a city, shopping and food, the weather and clothes, illness and the body, invitations, and a holiday. 405 of the 500 words are that vocabulary, together with the members of the categories it names without listing them (the days of the week, the months, the seasons, the numbers) and the pronouns, question words and connectives its A1 grammar list names. The programme presents its themes as suggestions rather than a fixed list, so this is not an official word list and is not presented as one. The other 95 are the commonest words of everyday Turkish, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 10 two-word expressions, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Turkish builds words by adding suffixes, and a suffix's vowel follows the vowels of the word (vowel harmony) while some stems change before it, so the card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 224 nouns show their plural and five cases — çocuk: çocuklar, çocuğu, çocuğa, çocukta, çocuktan, çocuğun. 71 verbs show the third person of the present, the aorist (the general present), the past and the future — etmek: ediyor, eder, etti, edecek — the aorist's vowel being the one a learner cannot predict. 12 pronouns show their cases. Adjectives do not inflect and carry no forms. Real example sentences come with 500 of the 500 words, three apiece for 496, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Scope: Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı, Türkiye Maarif Vakfı, 2020 (ISBN 978-605-80438-2-4). Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
